draft.title: Counterexamples
card: A counterexample is one case where a statement about all values fails. Finding a single counterexample proves the statement is false.
Many examples that work do not prove a statement true. A statement is only proved true for every case by a proof.
To disprove a claim, pick a value that makes the conditions true but the conclusion false, then check it by working it out.
Worked example: "n² + n + 41 is prime for every whole number n." Try n = 41: 41² + 41 + 41 = 41 × 43 = 1763. This is not prime, so n = 41 is a counterexample.
draft.remember: One failing case disproves a claim for all. Many working cases never prove it.

a.q: Claim: "n² > n for every whole number n." Which value of n is a counterexample?
a.why: For n = 1, n² = 1 and n = 1, so n² > n is false. For n = 2, 3 and 10 the claim holds (4 > 2, 9 > 3, 100 > 10), so they cannot disprove it.
a.clue: Which value makes both sides equal?

b.q: Mia claims that "if n is a prime number, then n + 2 is also prime". She checks n = 3, 5 and 11 and finds it works each time. What does this show?
opts: Nothing is proved, and n = 7 disproves the claim
The claim is proved, because three cases work
The claim is proved, because 3, 5 and 11 are all odd
Nothing is proved, and n = 11 disproves the claim
b.why: For n = 3, 5 and 11 the claim holds, but working cases never prove it for all primes. For n = 7, n + 2 = 9 = 3 × 3, which is not prime, so n = 7 is a counterexample. For n = 11, n + 2 = 13 is prime, so n = 11 does not disprove it.

b.best: Nothing is proved, and n = 7 disproves the claim
